How it happens in polished/src/game/main.js:

- `sail()` resets W at line 92 with `Object.assign(W, {n:0, state:'calm', timer:5, lost:0, choose:0, sunk:false})`, which leaves out `next`. The initializer at line 69 doesn't have it either.
- The "Back to port" button (line 240) runs only when `W.state === 'choose'`, which is exactly the moment line 225 has just filled `W.next`. `endVoyage` (lines 103-111) doesn't clear it.
- The next voyage starts from the port's Set sail button (port.js:144, `onSail` → `sail`). After 5 s, line 211 runs `W.next ?? waveAt(W.n…)` and spawns the leftover wave. The banner uses `W.n + 1`, so it says "wave 1".
- Example: bank after beating wave 4 and `W.next = waveAt(4)` = `{ids:['brig'], captain:0}`. The next voyage, even in a Skiff, opens with "Wave 1: a raider captain", a captain Brig with double toughness.

The same leak happens on two more paths:
- Pause, then "Back to port" (line 255) while the card is up.
- The same, during the 4 s calm after "Sail on". `W.next` is still set until the wave spawns.

Why it breaks the check (tools/check.mjs):
- At line 157 the flown block forces wave 15 (state becomes 'fight'). The treasure-ship test (lines 160-163) then clears the raiders and spawns one prize. When she strikes, no raider is left standing, so lines 218-225 run: `W.n=15, state='choose', W.next=waveAt(15)`.
- WAVES has 15 entries, so `waveAt(15)` draws 3 random ships from the 11-ship pool. The runner's 15 s step doesn't use up the 25 s choose timer, so `W.next` survives.
- The whole-voyage block (lines 200-225) then clicks Set sail in the same page. `sail()` keeps the leftover, so the Skiff's "wave 1" is 3 random ships and the 200 s loop can time out.
- That fits the earlier agent's numbers: 2 of 3 runs failed, and 3 of 3 passed once `W.next` was cleared.

Where the claim overreaches:
- The "red damage vignette flashes" part doesn't hold up. `#hurt` sits inside `#hud` (demos/game.html:289-324), and `#hud` is hidden in title and port mode.
- In voyage mode, `frame()` runs `tick()`, which rewrites `#hurt`'s opacity (line 319), before the first render and paint.
- `cam.shake` wears off within 0.3 s.
- Resetting `hurt` and `cam.shake` is harmless tidying, not part of the bug. `V` is already reset in `sail()`.

Smallest fix in polished/src/game/main.js:
1. Line 69: `const W = { n: 0, state: 'calm', timer: 5, lost: 0, choose: 0, sunk: false, next: null };`
2. Line 92, in `sail()`: add `next: null` to the reset, i.e. `Object.assign(W, { n: 0, state: 'calm', timer: 5, lost: 0, choose: 0, sunk: false, next: null });`. This one change covers all three ways out: the card's "Back to port", pause then "Back to port", and sinking.

Making the check catch it again (tools/check.mjs):
- In the whole-voyage block (around line 207), note `g.raiders.list.map(r => r.id)` the first time the list has raiders. Report the problem "wave 1 should be one Skiff, got …" unless it is exactly `['skiff']`.

Code path (polished/src/game):
- **Why it can happen.** port.js keeps one `ship` on show. `show(id)` (lines 64-77) only takes out of the port scene the ship it had on show before (line 68: `if (ship && ship !== next) scene.remove(ship.root)`). It never touches the voyage scene. Clicking a ship you don't own only sets `viewing` (lines 120-124). It does not change `flying`. And `#btn-sail` sits outside `#pp-own` in demos/game.html (line 285), so "Set sail in the Zephyr" stays visible while you look at a ship you don't own.
- **Step 1, sail while looking at another ship.** `sail()` in main.js line 86 does `scene.add(ship.root)`. That moves the Zephyr (skiff) root into the voyage scene. The port scene keeps the Gale (cutter).
- **Step 2, come home.** `endVoyage()` (main.js 103-112) clears raiders, bolts and pickups but never the player ship. Its `port.setMode('port')` calls `show('cutter')`. The port ship is already the cutter, so nothing is removed, and the Zephyr root stays a child of the voyage scene.
- **Step 3, buy and sail.** `#btn-buy` (port.js 128-132) sets `flying = cutter` and does not call `show`. `sail('cutter')` then re-parents the Gale into the voyage scene. The Zephyr is still there.
- **Only fix in play today.** The ghost goes away only if the player later shows that same ship in port (its ship button, or the title screen while it is the ship being flown). three.js `add()` re-parents, so that fixes it.

Browser run (dist/game.html, 400x800, steps: reset, To port, tap the Gale, Set sail, Pause, Back to port, give 1000 shards, Buy, Set sail):
- First voyage: the voyage scene held ["Zephyr"].
- Back in port: the voyage scene still held ["Zephyr"]. The port scene held ["Gale"].
- Second voyage: the voyage scene held ["Zephyr","Gale"], and the point lights went from 1 to 2.

This is the natural way a new player moves up: look at the next ship, find it too dear, sail, earn shards, come home to that ship still on show, buy it, sail.

What the player gets:
- A full-detail ship frozen where the last voyage ended. It stays tilted if she was sinking, and it has no tag.
- Draw calls and about 100k triangles whenever it is in view.
- Its lamp(s) are always counted in the light loop. three.js gathers every visible light in the scene, not only the ones on screen. That brings one shader recompile and per-pixel cost on a phone.
- Ghosts can pile up, one per ship flown this way.

tools/check.mjs also leaves ghosts, because `voyage(id)` at line 105 calls `g.fly()` for several ships in a row with no `endVoyage`. It asserts nothing about this, so the check still passes.

The claim's "high" rating is a little strong for what you see. Starts are random on a 2,500 m circle, so the ghost is often a far speck. But the bug is real and easy to reach.
fix:
Make two one-line changes in polished/src/game/main.js. three.js `Object3D.remove` does nothing if the object isn't a child of that scene, so both lines are safe whichever scene the root is in at the time.

1. In `endVoyage(keep)` (line 103), before `port.setMode('port')`, add `scene.remove(player.ship.root);`. A voyage then leaves no player ship behind in the voyage scene. `port.show(viewing)` on the very next line puts the root into the port scene if that ship is the one on show. This covers every way back to port in normal play: Back to port between waves, Back to port from the pause menu, and after sinking.
2. In `sail(id, force)` (line 76), before `player = makeFlyer(...)` replaces the old flyer, add `if (player && player.ship !== ship) scene.remove(player.ship.root);`. This covers calling `__game.fly()` twice in a row with no trip to port, as tools/check.mjs does at line 105.

Optionally, harden tools/check.mjs:
- After a port round trip that switches ships, check that the voyage scene holds exactly one full-detail ship root. For example: Zephyr voyage, then endVoyage, then buy the cutter, then sail it, then count `scene.children` that are Groups whose name is one of the SHIPS names, and expect 1.

reasoning:
The repeated work is real. The claim that it is the single biggest GPU cost on phones is a guess and could not be measured here.

Code path (polished/src/game/world.js):
- CLOUD_GLSL (lines 56-61): each cover() runs 2 fbm x 5 octaves x 4 fract(sin) hashes, so 40 sin() calls.
- shade() (lines 79-88) puts one cover() into every ground material at map_fragment.
- The sea (lines 97-98) is a 160 km plane that also goes through shade(). It is opaque but has depthWrite:false and renderOrder -5, so three.js draws it first, under the whole map. Nothing is in front of it yet, so early depth tests can't skip any of its pixels. The nine opaque tiles then draw over it at the same y=0 and also run cover(). Inside the map, the sea's cover() is wasted work.
- The deck (lines 105-108) is a transparent 160 km plane at y=430 with no discard. It runs cover() twice ('c' and 'lit') on every pixel below the horizon.

Ships fly between 60 and 2400 m, and the camera sits about 700 m up with pitch 0.2 (fov 68 in portrait), so the deck always fills the lower screen. Per ground pixel: 4 cover() inside the map, 3 outside. That's 160 or 120 sin() calls, at pixel ratio 1.6 (624x1350).

The ground's share of the screen checks out. A phone-size screenshot shows about 65% ground and deck, about 15% ship (scratchpad/survey/f02-cloud-noise/phone-base.png).

Measurement: headless SwiftShader at the check's phone size (624x1350), 4 frames x 3 rounds, script scratchpad/survey/f02-cloud-noise/measure.mjs. Materials were patched at runtime only; no repo files were touched. Captain's ship hidden so only the world is timed:
- as now: 126-140 ms
- sea without cloud shadows: about 120 ms
- also one cover() on the deck: 97-118 ms
- no cloud noise at all: 75-81 ms
- baked-texture version (2 texture fetches per cover): 80-95 ms
- sky only: about 27 ms

So the noise is about 40% of the world's draw time and about half the ground's. A baked texture gets almost all of that back.

Limits of the measurement:
- With the 100k-triangle ship visible, SwiftShader frames take 550-1000 ms. Vertex and shadow work on the CPU dominates there, so SwiftShader can't show that the noise is the biggest cost on a phone GPU.
- On a tile-based phone GPU, vertex work is cheap and fragment work is what costs. The claim's figure of about 1,000-1,500 operations per pixel on about 0.55 MP is plausible, so it is very likely a large share. Still, it is an estimate, not a phone measurement.
- The hash-precision side claim (sin at arguments up to about 1e6 on some mobile GPUs) was not checked on hardware. It would mainly hit the low-weight high octaves.

Two parts of the proposed fix are wrong:
1. Baking a periodic fbm does not reproduce the current pattern exactly. The current noise doesn't repeat, and lacunarity 2.07 isn't a whole number, so the result is a similar but different pattern. That's fine visually.
2. Turning off sea shadows on touch would leave a visible line on the open sea where the map's shadowed painted sea meets the plain sea plane. Once the noise is baked, the sea's shadows cost only two fetches, so keep them.
fix:
In src/game/world.js, bake the cloud noise once and sample it everywhere.

1. In makeWorld, build one tileable noise texture in JS at load (about 20-40 ms on a phone, done once):
   - A THREE.DataTexture of 512x512, RedFormat, UnsignedByte.
   - Value-noise fbm over a period of P = 8 units of p, which is 8/0.00045, about 17.8 km.
   - Give each octave a whole-number lattice period: round(P * 2.07^k) cells, with lattice indices wrapped modulo that, so the texture tiles exactly. Keep 5 octaves, amplitude 0.5 halving each octave, and the +13.3 offset as a lattice shift.
   - wrapS and wrapT set to RepeatWrapping, generateMipmaps true, minFilter LinearMipmapLinearFilter, magFilter Linear. Mipmaps also stop the far deck from shimmering, which the procedural version does now.
   - Make one shared uniform object: const cloudU = { value: tex }.

2. Replace the body of CLOUD_GLSL (lines 56-61) with:
   uniform sampler2D uCloud;
   float cover(vec2 xz, float t) { vec2 p = xz * 0.00045 + vec2(t * 0.0022, t * 0.0009); return smoothstep(0.44, 0.64, texture2D(uCloud, p / 8.0).r * 0.85 + texture2D(uCloud, (p * 3.3 + 7.0) / 8.0).r * 0.25); }
   Drop h2, n2 and fbm.
   - In shade() (line 81), add sh.uniforms.uCloud = cloudU.
   - In the deck's uniforms (line 104), add uCloud: cloudU.
   - Keep the deck's 'lit' sample (2 more fetches; measured the same cost as without it) and keep the sea's cloud shadows. Don't turn sea shadows off on touch: it would leave a line where shadows stop at the map's edge.
   - Bump customProgramCacheKey to 'ground-cloud-shadow-2'.

3. Optional extra: stop the sea drawing under the map at all. Build it as four strips around the map instead of one 160 km plane, with the inner edge pulled about 100 m inside the map edge. The sea is drawn first and doesn't write depth, so the overlap can't flicker. This also avoids T-junction cracks.

Measured in SwiftShader at phone size, world only: 126-140 ms now, 80-95 ms with the texture, 75-81 ms with no noise at all.

Check afterwards with node tools/check.mjs (must end "all good"), and look at the deck and the ground shadows in the phone-size battle pictures. They should still line up, because the same cover() feeds both.

reasoning:
I couldn't refute this one. It happens on every voyage, for every ship the Captain can sail.

What the code does:
- polished/src/game/main.js:404 puts the sun at player.pos + SUN*400 every frame and aims sun.target at the player.
- sail() (main.js:87-88) sets the shadow camera to an orthographic box r = 0.85*L wide, with near 1 and far r*8.
- In three 0.186.1, LightShadow.updateMatrices (node_modules/three/src/lights/LightShadow.js:213-224) places the shadow camera at the light and points it at the target. DirectionalLightShadow does not override this. So the player sits at depth 400, while the camera only sees from 1 to r*8 metres.
- For the four ships the Captain can sail, far is 54 m (Skiff, L=8), 102 m (Cutter, 15), 170 m (Brig, 25) and 272 m (Frigate, 40). The Galleon and Man-o'-war are raiders only.

I checked this with a short node script that runs three's own updateMatrices (scratchpad/survey/f05/check.mjs). The player's shadowCoord.z comes out as 7.47, 3.95, 2.36 and 1.47, and frustum.intersectsSphere(ship) is false for all four ships. In the shader (shadowmap_pars_fragment), frustumTest needs shadowCoord.z <= 1.0. So every pixel of the ship is drawn fully lit. The ship is also culled from the shadow pass, so nothing is ever written into the shadow map. The ship never shades itself: no sail or rigging shadows on deck.

This is a mistake, not a choice. The port (port.js:75-77) uses the same pattern correctly: r = 0.9L, light about 2.4L away, far = 6r = 5.4L, so the ship sits inside the box. The voyage copied the box size but used a fixed 400 m distance.

Two parts of the claim go too far:
1. "Every lit pixel samples it" is wrong. The five PCF texture reads sit inside if(frustumTest). That test fails the same way for every pixel, so the reads are skipped. What is wasted each frame is a 2048² (laptop) or 1024² (phone) depth clear, the shadow-pass scene traversal, and a few shader operations per pixel. That is a small cost, not a large one.
2. PCFSoftShadowMap (main.js:40) only gives a one-time console warning in r186 (WebGLShadowMap.js:99-102) and falls back to PCF. tools/check.mjs counts only console errors, so the check is not affected.

So the defect is real and visible: the self-shadows were intended and never appear. The performance waste is small. Fixing it adds real cost: the player's full-detail ship (about 100k triangles) is drawn a second time into the shadow map every frame.
fix:
Smallest fix, one line, no new state: in sail() at polished/src/game/main.js:88, frame the depth range around where the light already sits:
  Object.assign(sun.shadow.camera, { left: -r, right: r, top: r, bottom: -r, near: 400 - r * 2, far: 400 + r * 2 });
Line 404 stays as it is. The player then lands at shadowCoord.z = 0.5. The depth range is 4r instead of 8r, so depth precision is better too. The existing bias (-0.0004, about 5 cm for the Frigate) and normalBias (0.04 m, about one texel of 2r/2048) are the values the port and hangar already use at a similar size.

Another way: keep near 1 / far r*8 and move the light to player.pos + SUN*(r*4). That needs r stored in sail() (for example sun.userData.r = r) and read at line 404, so it is a bigger change than the one above.

Also:
1. main.js:40: use THREE.PCFShadowMap. This drops the r186 console warning and looks the same, because three already falls back to it.
2. Phones: once the fix is in, the shadow pass really draws the full-detail player ship every frame. Measure the phone frame time. If it drops, set sun.castShadow = !touch at main.js:55, rather than renderer.shadowMap.enabled = false, so the port keeps its berth shadows on phones. Switching it off on phones also removes the wasted clear that happens there today. Don't refresh the shadow map only every other frame: three updates the shadow matrices only while it renders the map, so a skipped frame leaves the shadow lagging behind the moving ship.
3. After the change, run node tools/closeups.mjs frigate and node tools/closeups.mjs skiff, and look at a voyage shot for acne on the sails and hull, and for sails casting solid rectangles where they should have holes. Then run npm run check, which must still end with "all good".
4. Optional: port.js:57 uses a 2048² key-light map on phones too. 1024 on touch would match the voyage, but that is a separate, small change.

Code paths (polished/src):
- guns.js update(), which runs every tick:
  - line 120: a new `put` closure, plus two array literals for every glow point.
  - line 122: `s.c.clone()` for every spark.
  - line 115: `b.p.clone()` and `V(size,size,len)` for every bolt.
  - lines 108, 112, 117: `splice` (which returns a new array) and `forEach`.
- guns.js fire() and spark(), lines 93-102: three new Colors for every bolt, and for every spark an object with two clones and a Color. Bolts and sparks live 0.2-3.2 s, so they survive a scavenge and get promoted.
- raiders.js shoot(), lines 197-207, runs for every ready battery on every raider each tick, even when it holds fire:
  - a new array literal;
  - muzzle() (guns.js 143-147): two clones plus an object;
  - intercept (guns.js 45): two clones;
  - reaches(): calls muzzle again, `aim.clone()`, and clampToArc's three new vectors.
- flight.js 96: `forward()` makes a new vector for every flyer every tick.

Measured from my scratch folder only (survey/f04/gc.mjs and prof.mjs; unminified build in survey/f04/game-dev.html):
- Setup: Frigate against 6 raiders with AI on, Captain firing all the time, no drawing.
- Allocation: the sampling heap profiler (counting objects freed by minor and major GC) gave 6.6 MB/s. guns.js itself was 3.8 MB/s (update 1.4, put 1.0, muzzle 0.58, clampToArc 0.35, bolt loop 0.19). Most of the 1.7 MB/s inside three.js Vector3/Color clone() also comes from guns.js and raiders.js. raiders.js itself was 0.39, main.js 0.30, flight.js 0.16, damage.js 0.12.
- With the shipped minified dist/game.html, scavenges freed 4.2-6.9 MB per game second.

Effect, measured in desktop headless Chromium:
- A scavenge every ~16-17 MB, which is about every 2.5-4 s of real play at 60 fps.
- Most scavenges took 0.6-1.5 ms. One took 5.5 ms while the CPU was shared with another agent.
- About 80 KB/s gets promoted, which leads to incremental major GCs (one finalization pause was 2.4 ms).
- On a mid-range phone (about 3-5x slower JS, and probably smaller young-generation space so more frequent scavenges), expect pauses of a few ms every second or two in big fights. That will sometimes drop a frame when the frame is already close to budget.

So the allocation rate and the GC churn really happen in normal fights, on a laptop and on a phone. But the claimed 5-20 ms major-GC pauses are not supported. Most of the pause work is concurrent or incremental. Treat this as low-medium severity: a performance cleanup, not a visible bug.

Two of the claim's details are also correct:
- The spark cap is GMAX - max = 500. When it is full, spark() drops new sparks silently.
- tools/check.mjs reads and sets `g.bolts.bolts.length` (lines 246, 251, 254, 297), so any pooling has to keep `bolts.bolts` as a plain array of live bolts.
fix:
A minimal fix that keeps the same behaviour and keeps check.mjs passing (polished/src).

1. guns.js colours
- Add shared constants:
  - `const BODY = { player: new THREE.Color(BOLT_COLORS.player), raider: new THREE.Color(BOLT_COLORS.raider) }`
  - `HEAD[o] = BODY[o].clone().lerp(white, 0.3)`
- In fire(), set `b.color = BODY[owner] ?? BODY.player` and `b.head = HEAD[...]`. No new Color per bolt.

2. guns.js bolt pool
- Keep a free list: `const freeB = []`.
- fire(): `const b = freeB.pop() ?? { p: new THREE.Vector3(), prev: new THREE.Vector3(), v: new THREE.Vector3() }`. Fill it with `copy`/`set`, using scratch vectors for the spread and the inherit-or-zero velocity.
- Remove with swap-remove: `bolts[i] = bolts[bolts.length - 1]; bolts.pop(); freeB.push(b);`
- `bolts.bolts` stays an array of live bolts. check.mjs sets its length to 0; that only drops pooled objects, which later get allocated again.

3. guns.js spark pool
- Same idea: `freeS` objects that hold `p` and `v` Vector3s and plain numbers `r, g, b, life, max, size`.
- spark() copies p and v into them and sets the colour through one scratch Color with `setHex`.
- Remove sparks with swap-remove.
- In fire() and burst(), pass scratch vectors instead of `V(0,0,0)` and `d.clone()...`. spark() copies them, so this is safe.

4. guns.js update()
- Use indexed for-loops, with no `put` closure and no array literals. Write each point straight into the buffers:
  - `const j = n * 3; gpos[j] = p.x; gpos[j + 1] = p.y; gpos[j + 2] = p.z;`
  - for sparks: `gcol[j] = s.r * k` (and the same for g and b);
  - `gsize[n] = ...`
- In the instance loop, use two scratch vectors:
  - `tp.copy(b.p).addScaledVector(sc, -len / 2)`
  - `ts.set(b.K.size, b.K.size, len)`
  - then `m4.compose(tp, q, ts)`

5. guns.js helpers take an out-parameter
- `intercept(from, sv, target, tv, speed, out = new THREE.Vector3())`, with a module-level scratch for `rel`.
- `clampToArc(want, axis, yawMax, pitchMax, out = new THREE.Vector3())`, with module-level scratch vectors for `f`, `side` and `h`.

6. guns.js makeGunnery
- muzzle(b) writes into one object per gunnery, `const M = { p: new V3(), d: new V3(), K: null }`, and returns it. That is safe: main.js aimFor and raiders.js shoot call it again only for the same battery.
- `reaches(b, aim, m = this.muzzle(b))` uses scratch vectors for `want` and for the arc result.
- fire() uses a scratch `want` and a scratch arc result. bolts.fire copies the direction.

7. raiders.js shoot()
- Hoist `const SIDES = ['bow', 'port', 'starboard', 'stern']`.
- Call `intercept(..., aimS)` with a module scratch vector (fire copies it).
- Pass `m` into `reaches(b, aim, m)`.

8. flight.js move()
- `s.velocity.set(Math.sin(s.heading) * s.speed, s.vy, Math.cos(s.heading) * s.speed)` instead of `forward()`.

Optional: raise GMAX (900 to about 1200) so big fights stop dropping sparks.

Expected result:
- The guns.js and raiders.js paths fall from about 4.5-5.5 MB/s to under 0.3 MB/s.
- About 1 MB/s is left, from hud/tags strings, steer() objects, firstHit and similar. The claim's "under 100 KB/s" is not realistic without also changing those.
- Scavenges would come about every 15-20 s instead of every 2-4 s.

How to check:
- Rerun survey/f04/gc.mjs against a scratch build ("freed MB per sim second").
- `node tools/check.mjs` must still end with "all good".

I read the code and ran a short headless test. Both parts of the claim are real. The second part is cosmetic.

**Code path (polished/src/game/main.js)**
- `resize()` (lines 266-274) sets the minimap's backing size from `mini.getBoundingClientRect()` (line 272).
- `#minimap` sits inside `#hud` (demos/game.html lines 289-350). That block is `display:none` whenever `body[data-mode='title']` or `body[data-mode='port']` (game.html line 40).
- The first `resize()` (line 276) runs before `port.setMode('title')` (line 277), while `data-mode` is still unset. So the first measurement is right. That is why the bug never shows on a fresh load.
- Any later window resize on the title screen or in port measures 0x0, and the backing size is set to 0x0.
- Setting sail (`sail()` lines 75-102, then `enter('voyage')`) never calls `resize()` again.
- `hud()` (lines 359-367) reads `mini.width`/`mini.height` as-is and draws into a 0x0 canvas. Nothing appears, so the player sees an empty blue box with a border for the whole voyage. It stays that way until a resize happens during the voyage.
- Each later return to port opens the same window for the bug again.

**Browser run** (scratch/survey/f06/run.mjs, laptop 1280x800, built dist/game.html; only the viewport was changed):

| Moment | Backing size | Shown size |
|---|---|---|
| After load (title) | 256x171 | 0x0 |
| After resizing to 1200x780 on the title screen | 0x0 | 0x0 |
| After `__game.fly('brig')` + `step(0.5)` | 0x0 | 240x160 |

Nothing could be drawn: the canvas has no pixels. After adding `.big`, the backing was still 0x0 but it was shown at 900x600.

**How players hit it**
- Turning a phone on the title screen or in port.
- The claude.ai artifact frame or the iOS viewport settling after load.
- Resizing a laptop window, going fullscreen or opening devtools before setting sail.

tools/check.mjs never resizes a page, so the check does not catch this. It is still normal play on both a phone and a laptop.

**Big map**
- The click handler (line 262) and the 'm' key (line 378) only toggle the CSS class `.big` (game.html line 141: `width:min(92vw,900px)`). The canvas is never resized.
- On a 1280-wide laptop, the 768x512 map art is first shrunk to 256x171 and then stretched about 3.5x to 900x600. The result is a blurry, soft-edged big map, with the ship arrow and raider dots scaled up by the same amount.
- This one is cosmetic, but real.

The proposed fix (size the canvas lazily inside the 10 Hz part of `hud()`) is right and covers every case: resizes in any mode, the `.big` toggle, and a page that loads while its frame has zero size. I refined it slightly, as described in the fix.
fix:
1. Delete the minimap line from `resize()` in polished/src/game/main.js (line 272: `const r = mini.getBoundingClientRect(); mini.width = ...; mini.height = ...;`). Measuring there is what breaks it while the HUD is hidden.

2. In `hud()`, size the canvas just before drawing. Put this inside the `if (mimg.complete && mimg.naturalWidth) {` block (line 358), before `const W2 = mini.width, H2 = mini.height;`:

```js
const dpr = Math.min(devicePixelRatio, 2); // the map art is only 768x512; 2x keeps the arrow sharp without big canvases on 3x phones
const cw = Math.round(mini.clientWidth * dpr), ch = Math.round(mini.clientHeight * dpr);
if (cw && ch && (cw !== mini.width || ch !== mini.height)) { mini.width = cw; mini.height = ch; }
```

Notes on this:
- `clientWidth`/`clientHeight` measure the inside of the 2px border, which is what the canvas actually shows. `getBoundingClientRect` includes the border.
- The size only changes when it differs, so there is no cost on ordinary frames.
- Changing the size clears the canvas, but it is redrawn straight away in the same call.
- The `.big` toggle (click and the 'm' key) and every mode change are covered without extra code. Each runs at most 0.1 s with the old size.

3. Optional: in the click handler (line 262) and the 'm' branch (line 378), set `hudTimer = 0` after the toggle so the bigger map redraws sharp on the next frame instead of up to 100 ms later.

The claim gets the numbers a bit wrong. Lock tolerance is max(0.05, atan(0.8·length/along)), so it's often 0.08 to 0.12 rad at broadside range, not 0.05. How the code behaves (three 0.186.1):
- The page doesn't handle a lost drawing context itself. three.js does: on loss, WebGLRenderer.onContextLost calls preventDefault and stops drawing. On restore, onContextRestore runs initGLContext(), which starts a fresh properties store.
- After that, ordinary textures come back. WebGLTextures.setTexture2D (line 559) uploads them again because their __version no longer matches. That covers the ship art (materials.js line 69, built from images that stay in memory), the map tiles (TextureLoader) and the canvas textures.
- Render-target textures are left out of that path (isRenderTargetTexture === true). So the sky-light picture made by pmrem.fromScene(...) (main.js lines 49-51) ends up with no GPU texture. WebGLState.bindTexture then binds three's empty texture, which is all zeros, so the sky light reads as black.
- r186's fromScene() has no option to draw into an existing render target (only size and position), so the old texture object can't be refilled in place.
- port.js line 53 shares the same texture object, so the title screen and the port lose the light too.
- Nothing else in src/ uses a render target. The shadow maps are redrawn every frame, so the sky light is the only thing that stays broken.

The claim is real. The line number is wrong: polished/src/game/progress.js has 69 lines and is identical to src/game/progress.js. connect() is at lines 39-52, push() at 53-61 and save() at 65.

How it happens: connect() reads data/users/<id>/save once, at page load. After that, save() stamps the tab's in-memory copy with Date.now(), and push() calls remote.set() with it blindly. Nothing ever reads the store again or subscribes to it. Every progress change goes through save(): the skies buttons (port.js:106), picking a ship (port.js:120), buying (port.js:128), the crystal-power slider (port.js:131), upgrades (port.js:140) and banking shards at the end of a voyage (main.js:105). So an old open tab writes its stale copy over newer progress with a newer stamp. Any other device that loads afterwards sees the store as newer and takes it (line 49). This is normal play: the game is published with db and user, and docs/game.md line 49 promises the save "follows you to another device". Chris uses both a phone and a laptop.

I checked it with a two-device simulation in Node. It runs the real progress.js in separate vm contexts (separate localStorage on each device) and shares one fake per-user store (scratchpad/survey/f09-verify/sim.mjs). Steps: the laptop banks 1000 shards and stays open. The phone loads, buys the Brig and banks 700 (store: 800 shards, Brig owned). Back on the laptop, Chris taps a skies button, and the store goes back to 1000 shards with no Brig. When the phone reloads it takes that copy, so the Brig and the voyage are gone on both devices.

A second path the claim doesn't mention, also confirmed (race.mjs): a save made before connect() has answered (for example, tapping a skies button on the title screen while use()/user.id()/get() are still pending). That bumps data.saved past the store's stamp, so connect() pushes the old local save over newer progress from the other device. Clock skew between devices fails the same way.

Not affected: tools/check.mjs and sim-fight. There is no window.claude in headless Chromium, so connect() returns at line 40 and the check can't see this bug. Medium severity is fair: it needs two devices, but the loss can't be undone.

The proposed fix (get() before each set(), plus connect() again on visibilitychange) is right in spirit but incomplete. It doesn't handle saves made before the first connect, and calling connect() repeatedly would open more subscriptions. The db API (contract 0.2.69, db.d.ts:417) has onSnapshot, with live delivery or a ~30 s refresh as fallback, and no transactions. So the better fix is: subscribe once, keep a "last synced" stamp, and let the store win whenever it changed since this device last synced. I tested a patched copy (scratchpad/survey/f09-verify/progress-fixed.js, harness.mjs) in four scenarios: a stale tab, an early tap, offline play then reconnect, and a phone clock 1 h slow. The current code loses progress in all four; the patched copy keeps it in all four.
fix:
In polished/src/game/progress.js (all of this goes inside makeProgress; one subscription; it never writes from a snapshot callback, in line with db.d.ts):

1. Add `synced: 0` to fresh(). It is the `saved` stamp of the store copy this device last read or wrote, and it is kept in localStorage alongside the save. data.saved > data.synced means this device has changes the store hasn't got yet.

2. Add helpers:
```js
function adopt(d) { data = merge(fresh(), JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(d))); data.synced = data.saved; writeLocal(); for (const f of listeners) f(data); }
const news = (d) => d && (d.saved ?? 0) > data.synced && d.saved !== data.saved; // someone else wrote since we last synced
```

3. In connect(), replace line 49-50 with:
```js
if (news(d)) adopt(d); else if (data.saved > data.synced) push();
ref.onSnapshot((s) => { const n = s.exists ? s.data() : null; if (!writing && news(n)) adopt(n); }, () => {});
```
The store wins whenever it changed since this device last synced. That fixes the early-tap race and stale local saves, while offline-only changes still get pushed when the store hasn't moved. The subscription brings the other device's saves into an open tab live; port.js:219 onLoad already refreshes the port, and endVoyage/sail read progress.data fresh, so adopting mid-voyage just banks the voyage onto the newer data.

4. In push(), take one last look before writing:
```js
if (!remote || data.saved <= data.synced) return; ...
const snap = await remote.get(), d = snap.exists ? snap.data() : null;
if (news(d)) adopt(d); else { const out = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(data)); await remote.set(out); data.synced = out.saved; writeLocal(); }
```
Keep the existing writing/again/error-code handling. This covers a tab whose snapshot stream was paused while it was in the background.

5. Use a stamp that can't go backwards: `save() { data.saved = Math.max(Date.now(), data.synced + 1, data.saved + 1); writeLocal(); push(); }`. A device with a slow clock still writes a newer stamp than the one it last saw.

6. reset() must keep the sync stamp, or the store would bring the old save straight back: `reset() { const s = data.synced; data = fresh(); data.synced = s; this.save(); }`.

Optional: in main.js, add progress.onLoad(() => note('Progress from your other device is loaded')) so Chris sees why his numbers changed. Old saves have no `synced` field, so it becomes 0 and the store's copy wins once on first load, which is the safe default. tools/check.mjs is unaffected (no window.claude in headless Chromium). The two-device harness in scratchpad/survey/f09-verify/harness.mjs could become a small tools/ check, because the browser check can't test this.

reasoning: Real, but much narrower than claimed. Chromium already skips writes that don't change anything: textContent set to the same single text, an unchanged inline style value, an unchanged className/classList. The whole game tick (JS only) is 0.8-1.3 ms on this machine, so it's a noticeable share, and a phone is several times slower. The `[...children].some` scan (line 314) is trivial.

reasoning: Real, but the smallest win in this list. Every frame sets needsUpdate with no update ranges on: bolt matrices and colours (guns.js:118), the 900-point glow buffers (guns.js:124), the smoke attributes (effects.js:44) and the pickups (pickups.js:56-57). three 0.186.1's WebGLAttributes then calls `gl.bufferSubData(target, 0, array)` with the whole array. That's about 25.6 + 4.8 + 25.2 + 21.6 + 12.8 + 2.4 ≈ 92 KB per frame, even with nothing in flight. The arithmetic matches the claim. The real cost is probably well under 0.1 ms per frame (copies through the browser's command buffer). It's cheap to fix but low priority next to F10-F13 and F17.
fix: Upload only the live part, and nothing when it's empty. Example for the bolts (guns.js:118): `mesh.count = bolts.length; if (bolts.length) { mesh.instanceMatrix.clearUpdateRanges(); mesh.instanceMatrix.addUpdateRange(0, bolts.length * 16); mesh.instanceMatrix.needsUpdate = true; mesh.instanceColor.clearUpdateRanges(); mesh.instanceColor.addUpdateRange(0, bolts.length * 3); mesh.instanceColor.needsUpdate = true; }`. Do the same for the glows (n*3, n*3, n), the smoke (puffs.length*3 and puffs.length) and the pickups (list.length*16 and list.length*3). Never add a range with count 0: three passes the count as the WebGL2 bufferSubData length, and a length of 0 means 'to the end of the array', which is a full upload again. three clears the ranges after each upload by itself.
